mainTopic: Stories of shaky walls and the merit of צדיקים (רבי יוחנן and אילפא, נחום איש גם זו), and the definition of a plague
overview: The amud opens with the last words of an earlier story: רבא could not open his house to every hungry person, because מחוזא was full of soldiers. Next comes the story of אילפא and רבי יוחנן, who leave Torah study for business because they are poor. Angels nearly knock a shaky wall onto them, but they spare them because one of them has a great future. רבי יוחנן goes back to learning and becomes head of the ישיבה. אילפא then proves that he still knows his learning by answering a ברייתא with רבי מאיר's rule, מצוה לקיים דברי המת. The גמרא then tells about נחום איש גם זו. His merit kept a shaky house standing, and he explains that his terrible suffering was atonement he asked for after a poor man died waiting for food. The story of the stolen gift to the emperor shows why he always said 'גם זו לטובה'. Finally the גמרא returns to the משנה and uses a ברייתא to define a plague (דבר) by the size of the city and the pattern of deaths.

steps.title: Why רבא could not open his house to everyone
steps.stepSummary: The closing reason in רבא's statement: there are too many soldiers in מחוזא.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because there are many soldiers in מחוזא.
steps.whatsHappening: These are the last words of the previous story. רבא explains the one practice of רב הונא that he could not copy: inviting every needy person in to eat.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא said he could keep all of רב הונא's good practices except open hospitality. The reason is practical: מחוזא was full of soldiers, and if he opened his doors they would eat everything he owned. This line closes that story so the גמרא can move on.

keyTerms.meaning: מחוזא, רבא's city, a busy town on the Tigris

steps.confusionAlert: This line is the end of a story that started earlier. It is NOT part of the אילפא story that follows.

phrases.english: because there are many
soldiers in Meḥoza.
phrases.notes: If רבא let all of them in, they would eat up everything he had.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִשּׁוּם דִּנְפִישִׁי בְּנֵי חֵילָא דְּמָחוֹזָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes רבא's statement earlier.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: רבא could not copy רב הונא's open-door policy because of the many soldiers in מחוזא.

steps.title: Two poor scholars decide to go into business
steps.stepSummary: אילפא and רבי יוחנן are learning and very poor, so they decide to go into business.
steps.simpleTranslation: אילפא and רבי יוחנן were learning Torah and were in great financial distress. They said: Let us get up, go, do business, and fulfill for ourselves the פסוק 'Although there should be no needy among you.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a new story. It sets the scene: two great scholars are so poor that they decide to leave learning for business.
steps.deeperAnalysis: They quote a פסוק that speaks of having no poor people. They read it as permission to work so they will not stay paupers. This sets up the tension of the story: is leaving Torah study for a living the right choice?

keyTerms.meaning: אילפא, an אמורא who learned with רבי יוחנן
things were tight for them, meaning they were very poor

phrases.english: Ilfa and Rabbi Yoḥanan
were studying Torah,
and things became very tight for them,
they said: Let us get up and go
and do business
and fulfill with regard to ourselves
"Although there should be no needy among you" (Deuteronomy 15:4).
phrases.notes: They use the פסוק as a reason to earn a living.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִילְפָא וְרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן הֲווֹ גָּרְסִי בְּאוֹרָיְיתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new story, which is linked to the previous one by the theme of a shaky wall.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The two scholars choose business over learning because of poverty, and they cite אפס כי לא יהיה בך אביון.

steps.title: Sitting under a shaky wall, two angels arrive
steps.stepSummary: While eating under a crumbling wall, they are visited by two מלאכי השרת.
steps.simpleTranslation: They went and sat under a crumbling wall, and they were eating bread. Two ministering angels came.
steps.whatsHappening: The story continues and places them in danger. This step sets up the angels' conversation that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The crumbling wall is the danger point of the story. The angels' arrival tells us that heaven is about to judge their decision to leave learning.

phrases.english: They went and sat
under a crumbling wall,
they were eating bread,
and two ministering angels came.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲזַלוּ, אוֹתִיבוּ תּוּתֵי גּוּדָּא רְעִיעָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story by moving them into the scene of danger.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: They are physically at risk under a crumbling wall when the angels appear.

steps.title: One angel wants to punish them
steps.stepSummary: One angel proposes knocking the wall on them for abandoning eternal life for temporary life.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן heard one say to the other: Let us throw this wall on them and kill them, because they leave the life of the World to Come and busy themselves with temporary life!
steps.whatsHappening: The first angel attacks their decision. He says they deserve to die for leaving Torah study to make money.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The angel presents the opposite view to their פסוק: Torah is חיי עולם הבא, and business is only חיי שעה. Leaving the eternal for the temporary is treated as a serious failing. This is the 'challenge' against their choice.

keyTerms.meaning: temporary life, meaning earning a living

phrases.english: Rabbi Yoḥanan heard
that one said to his fellow:
Let us throw this wall on them
and kill them,
for they leave the life of the World to Come
and busy themselves with temporary life!

steps.triggerLanguage: שַׁמְעֵיהּ רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן דְּאָמַר חַד לְחַבְרֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The angels now judge the decision made in step 2.
steps.kashyaTarget: The scholars' decision to leave Torah study for business.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Giving up eternal Torah life for temporary livelihood is a grave wrong that deserves punishment.
steps.whyThisMatters: The pair חיי עולם הבא and חיי שעה is a classic way חז"ל contrast Torah study with worldly pursuits.

steps.title: The other angel says to spare them
steps.stepSummary: The second angel says to leave them, because one of them has a great destiny waiting.
steps.simpleTranslation: The other said to him: Leave them, because there is one among them whose time stands ready for him.
steps.whatsHappening: The second angel pushes back and saves them. He says one of them has a special future still waiting.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He does not argue that the first angel's reasoning is wrong. He gives a reason to spare them anyway: one of them is destined for greatness. The story is now set up to ask: which one?

keyTerms.meaning: his hour stands for him, meaning his time of greatness is still ahead

phrases.english: The other said to him: Leave them,
for there is one among them
whose hour stands ready for him.
phrases.notes: His moment of success has not yet come.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ אִידַּךְ: שַׁבְקִינְהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the first angel's proposal.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Exception: punishment is held back because of a future destiny.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both deserve death for leaving Torah.
steps.terutzMaskana: They are spared because one of them is destined for greatness.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן asks אילפא if he heard anything
steps.stepSummary: Only רבי יוחנן heard the angels, and he checks whether אילפא heard as well.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן heard; אילפא did not hear. רבי יוחנן said to אילפא: Did the master hear anything?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells us only one of them heard the angels. רבי יוחנן asks a question to find out which of them the angel meant.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The fact that only one of them heard becomes the clue. רבי יוחנן asks carefully, without saying what he heard, to test his theory.

keyTerms.meaning: master, a polite way to say 'you'

phrases.english: Rabbi Yoḥanan heard,
Ilfa did not hear.
Rabbi Yoḥanan said to Ilfa:
Did the master hear anything?

steps.triggerLanguage: שָׁמַע מָר מִידֵּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries to identify the 'one' mentioned by the second angel.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether אילפא also heard the angels.

steps.title: אילפא answers no
steps.stepSummary: אילפא did not hear anything.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: No.
steps.whatsHappening: אילפא answers the question: he heard nothing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This short answer is the key evidence. It confirms that the angels' words reached only רבי יוחנן.

phrases.english: He said to him: No.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: לָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 6.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן concludes the destiny is his
steps.stepSummary: Since only he heard, רבי יוחנן deduces that he is the one with the great future.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said: Since I heard and אילפא did not hear, learn from this that it is for me that the hour stands ready.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן draws a conclusion from the fact that only he heard. The message was meant for him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His reasoning is that a heavenly message reaches only the person it concerns. Because אילפא heard nothing, the 'one' whose time is coming must be רבי יוחנן.

keyTerms.meaning: learn from this; a standard phrase for drawing a conclusion

phrases.english: He said: Since I heard
and Ilfa did not hear,
learn from this
that it is for me that the hour stands ready.

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁמַע מִינַּהּ לְדִידִי קָיְימָא לִי שַׁעְתָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the conclusion from אילפא's answer.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: רבי יוחנן is the one with the destined future.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן decides to go back to learning
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן decides to return and accept poverty, citing the opposite פסוק.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said to him: I will go back, and I will fulfill for myself the פסוק 'For the poor shall never cease out of the land.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן changes course. He will return to Torah study even if it means staying poor.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier they quoted אפס כי לא יהיה בך אביון to justify going into business. Now רבי יוחנן quotes a פסוק from the same פרשה, כי לא יחדל אביון. It means he accepts being one of the poor so he can keep learning.

keyTerms.meaning: and I will apply to myself

steps.confusionAlert: Notice the two פסוקים mirror each other. The first was used to leave learning, and this one is used to come back.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yoḥanan said to him: I will go back,
and fulfill with regard to myself
"For the poor shall never cease out of the land" (Deuteronomy 15:11).

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: אֶיהֱדַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Acts on the conclusion of step 8 and reverses the decision of step 2.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי יוחנן chooses Torah with poverty over business.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן becomes head of the ישיבה
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן went back, אילפא did not, and by the time אילפא returned, רבי יוחנן had been appointed head.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן returned; אילפא did not return. By the time אילפא came back, רבי יוחנן had been appointed head of the ישיבה.
steps.whatsHappening: This shows the result of רבי יוחנן's choice: his return to learning led to his appointment as head of the ישיבה. The story is not over yet; the next steps turn to אילפא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The angel's words come true: the 'hour' waiting for רבי יוחנן was his leadership. Choosing Torah, even with poverty, led to greatness, and his finances improved as well.

keyTerms.meaning: was appointed, here meaning head of the ישיבה

steps.confusionAlert: מליך literally means 'reigned,' but here it means he was appointed head of the academy, not king.
steps.whatToRemember: Two scholars left learning because of poverty. Angels judged them, and only רבי יוחנן heard that someone's 'hour' was coming. He went back to Torah and became head of the ישיבה. The story praises staying with Torah study even when it is financially hard.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yoḥanan returned,
Ilfa did not return.
By the time Ilfa came back,
Rabbi Yoḥanan had been appointed head.

steps.triggerLanguage: עַד דַּאֲתָא אִילְפָא, מָלֵיךְ רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows the outcome of רבי יוחנן's decision.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The angel's prediction is fulfilled: רבי יוחנן returns to Torah and is appointed head of the ישיבה.

steps.title: אילפא's friends tease him about what he missed
steps.stepSummary: After רבי יוחנן was appointed head, the people tell אילפא that he would have been appointed if he had stayed and learned.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: If you had sat and learned, wouldn't you have been appointed?
steps.whatsHappening: The people turn to אילפא and point out what he lost by leaving to do business. This sets up his dramatic answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The line is a sharp rhetorical jab, not a real question. It suggests that אילפא's Torah knowledge is weaker because he left. He answers by publicly proving he still knows everything.

keyTerms.meaning: Master, a respectful way to address a Torah scholar

phrases.english: They said to him:
If the Master had sat and studied,
would the Master not have been appointed [head]?

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרוּ לוֹ: אִי אִתִּיב מָר וְגָרֵיס
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Reacts to the result in step 10, where רבי יוחנן was appointed head and אילפא was not.
steps.kashyaTarget: אילפא's choice to leave and pursue business
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Had he stayed to learn, he would have become head; leaving suggests he lost out, maybe even in knowledge.

steps.title: אילפא hangs from a ship's mast and issues a challenge
steps.stepSummary: אילפא hangs from a ship's mast and declares he will fall and drown if anyone asks him a ברייתא of רבי חייא and רבי אושעיא that he cannot explain from a משנה.
steps.simpleTranslation: He went and hung himself from the mast of a ship and said: If anyone asks me about a ברייתא of רבי חייא and רבי אושעיא and I cannot answer it from a משנה, I will fall from the mast and drown.
steps.whatsHappening: אילפא makes a dramatic public challenge to prove he still knows Torah well. This sets up the test question that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His claim is huge. He says every ברייתא in the big collections of רבי חייא and רבי אושעיא can be traced to a source in the משנה. He risks his life on it to show that his years in business did not make him forget his learning.

keyTerms.meaning: a ברייתא, a teaching outside the משנה

steps.confusionAlert: Here מַתְנִיתָא means a ברייתא (from רבי חייא and רבי אושעיא), while מַתְנִיתִין means our משנה. He is promising to trace the ברייתא back to the משנה.

phrases.english: He went and hung himself
from the mast of a ship,
he said: If there is anyone who asks me
about a baraita of Rabbi Chiya and Rabbi Oshaya
and I do not resolve it for him from a Mishnah,
I will fall from the mast of the ship and drown.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲזַל תְּלָא נַפְשֵׁיהּ בְּאַסְקַרְיָא דִסְפִינְתָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: אילפא's response to the jab in step 11.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: אילפא claims he can source every ברייתא of רבי חייא and רבי אושעיא in the משנה.

steps.title: An old man tests אילפא with a ברייתא about a father's will
steps.stepSummary: An old man quotes a ברייתא. If a dying father says to give his sons a shekel a week, they may get more if they need it. But if he said 'only a shekel,' or named other heirs after them, they get only a shekel.
steps.simpleTranslation: A certain old man came and taught him: One who says, 'Give my sons a shekel each week,' and they need a sela, they are given a sela. If he said, 'Give them only a shekel,' they are given only a shekel. If he said, 'If they die, others will inherit in their place,' then whether he said 'give' or 'give only,' they are given only a shekel.
steps.whatsHappening: The old man takes up אילפא's challenge by quoting a ברייתא. The hidden question is: where in the משנה does this come from?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא has three cases. A plain 'shekel' is read as an estimate, so the sons get what they need. 'Only a shekel' is a firm limit. Naming later heirs shows the father wants to save the rest of the money for them, so the sons get only a shekel even if he said just 'give.'

keyTerms.meaning: a coin, worth half a sela
others will inherit in their place

phrases.english: A certain old man came,
and taught him [a baraita]:
One who says: Give a shekel to my sons each week,
and they are fit to be given a sela
they give them a sela.

phrases.aramaic: וְאִם אָמַר: אַל תִּתְּנוּ לָהֶם אֶלָּא שֶׁקֶל
phrases.english: And if he said: Give them only a shekel
they give them only a shekel.
If he said: If they die,
others shall inherit in their place
whether he said 'Give'
or whether he said 'Give only'
they give them only a shekel.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲתָא הָהוּא סָבָא, תְּנָא לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Accepts אילפא's challenge from step 12 by presenting a ברייתא to be sourced.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which משנה, or whose view in the משנה, is the source of this ברייתא?

steps.title: אילפא answers: it follows רבי מאיר
steps.stepSummary: אילפא identifies the ברייתא as following רבי מאיר, who holds מצוה לקיים דברי המת.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Whose view is this? It is רבי מאיר, who said: It is a מצוה to carry out the words of a person who died.
steps.whatsHappening: אילפא passes the test. He traces the ברייתא to a known view in the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: All three cases come from one idea: we try to do exactly what the dead man wanted. That idea is רבי מאיר's rule, מצוה לקיים דברי המת. So the ברייתא has a clear source in the משנה, just as אילפא promised.

keyTerms.meaning: it is a מצוה to fulfill the wishes of the deceased

steps.whatToRemember: אילפא proved his learning was still sharp: he traced the ברייתא to רבי מאיר's principle מצוה לקיים דברי המת.

phrases.english: He said to him:
Whose is this? It is Rabbi Meir,
who said: It is a מצוה to fulfill the words of the dead.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: הָא מַנִּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the hidden question in step 13.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The ברייתא follows רבי מאיר: מצוה לקיים דברי המת.

steps.title: Describing נחום איש גם זו's suffering
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins a new story. נחום איש גם זו was blind, without hands or feet, and covered in boils, and he lay in a rundown house with his bed legs standing in water to keep ants away.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said about נחום איש גם זו that he was blind in both eyes, missing both hands, missing both legs, and his whole body was full of boils. He lay in a rundown house, and the legs of his bed stood in bowls of water so ants would not climb onto him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new story and first describes נחום's condition and his shaky house. This sets the scene for what happens next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two details matter for the story. First, the house is רעוע, about to fall. Second, נחום himself is a great צדיק despite his suffering. The story ties back to the earlier topic on the daf: not passing near a shaky wall, and the merit that can protect a person from danger.

keyTerms.meaning: נחום of Gam Zu, a תנא

phrases.aramaic: אָמְרוּ עָלָיו עַל נַחוּם אִישׁ גַּם זוֹ
phrases.english: They said about Nachum of Gam Zu
that he was blind in both his eyes,
missing both his hands,
missing both his legs,
and his whole body was full of boils.
And he was lying in a rundown house,

phrases.aramaic: וְרַגְלֵי מִטָּתוֹ מוּנָּחִין בִּסְפָלִין שֶׁל מַיִם
phrases.english: and the legs of his bed were placed in bowls of water
so that ants would not climb onto him.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרוּ עָלָיו עַל נַחוּם אִישׁ גַּם זוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new story, linked to the daf's broader theme of rundown buildings and protective merit.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Description of נחום איש גם זו's suffering and his rundown house.

steps.title: נחום tells his students to take out his things before his bed
steps.stepSummary: His students want to move his bed out first, but נחום tells them to take out the כלים first, promising that the house will not fall while he is inside.
steps.simpleTranslation: Once his students wanted to take out his bed first and then the כלים. He said to them: My sons, take out the כלים first and then my bed, because I promise you that as long as I am in the house, the house will not fall.
steps.whatsHappening: נחום reverses his students' plan and makes a bold promise. This prepares for the outcome in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The students naturally wanted to save their רבי first. נחום was sure that his own merit protected the house. So he told them to save the belongings while he was still inside, keeping the house standing.

keyTerms.meaning: you are guaranteed, I promise you

phrases.aramaic: פַּעַם אַחַת בִּקְּשׁוּ תַּלְמִידָיו לְפַנּוֹת מִטָּתוֹ,
phrases.english: Once his students sought to remove his bed,
and afterward remove the vessels.
He said to them: My sons,
remove the vessels,
and afterward remove my bed,
for you are guaranteed

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁכׇּל זְמַן שֶׁאֲנִי בַּבַּיִת אֵין הַבַּיִת נוֹפֵל.
phrases.english: that as long as I am in the house, the house will not fall.

steps.triggerLanguage: פַּעַם אַחַת בִּקְּשׁוּ תַּלְמִידָיו לְפַנּוֹת מִטָּתוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story begun in step 15.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: נחום promises that his presence keeps the house from collapsing.

steps.title: The house falls right after נחום is taken out
steps.stepSummary: The students take out the כלים, then the bed, and the house collapses.
steps.simpleTranslation: They took out the כלים, then they took out his bed, and the house fell.
steps.whatsHappening: The story ends by showing that נחום's promise came true.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The house held up only while נחום was inside. As soon as he was out, it fell. This proves his merit had been holding it up.
steps.whatToRemember: The merit of a צדיק like נחום איש גם זו can hold back danger. The shaky house stood until he left it.
steps.whyThisMatters: It sets up the students' next question: why did such a great צדיק suffer so much? His answer is the story of the poor man who died while waiting (steps 19-21). The 'גם זו לטובה' story comes later, in answer to a separate question about his name (step 22).

phrases.english: They removed the vessels
and afterward they removed his bed,
and the house fell.

steps.triggerLanguage: פִּינּוּ אֶת הַכֵּלִים וְאַחַר כָּךְ פִּינּוּ אֶת מִטָּתוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows the outcome of נחום's promise in step 16.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: נחום's merit protected the house. It fell only after he was removed.

steps.title: The students ask why a righteous man suffers
steps.stepSummary: The students ask נחום why he suffers so badly if he is a צדיק גמור.
steps.simpleTranslation: His students said to him: רבי, since you are completely righteous, why did this happen to you?
steps.whatsHappening: The students have just seen the house stay standing until נחום left it. Now they ask why someone that holy is blind, has no hands or feet, and is covered in boils.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The miracle of the house proved he is a צדיק גמור. So his terrible condition seems to contradict that. The question sets up his explanation.

phrases.english: His students said to him:
Rabbi, but since
you are a completely righteous man,
why did this happen to you?

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרוּ לוֹ תַּלְמִידָיו רַבִּי וְכִי מֵאַחַר שֶׁצַּדִּיק גָּמוּר אַתָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Reacts to the miracle of the house collapsing only after he left.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why a צדיק גמור would suffer such terrible afflictions.

steps.title: נחום caused it himself: the poor man who died waiting
steps.stepSummary: נחום says he brought the suffering on himself. He tells them how a poor man asked him for food and died while נחום was unloading his donkey.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said: My sons, I brought it on myself. Once I was traveling to my father-in-law's house with three donkeys loaded with food, drink, and delicacies. A poor man stopped me and asked for food. I told him to wait until I unloaded the donkey. Before I finished, he died.
steps.whatsHappening: נחום answers the students. He tells the story of the poor man he made wait.
steps.deeperAnalysis: נחום had plenty of food with him, three donkeys' worth. His delay was small and well-meant, but a man died because of it. נחום holds himself fully responsible even for that.

keyTerms.meaning: His soul left him; he died

phrases.english: He said to them: My sons,
I brought it upon myself.
For once I was traveling
on the road to my father-in-law's house,
and I had with me the load of three donkeys,

phrases.aramaic: אֶחָד שֶׁל מַאֲכָל, וְאֶחָד שֶׁל מִשְׁתֶּה,
phrases.english: one of food, and one of drink,
and one of delicacies.
A poor man came
and stood before me on the road,
and said to me: Rabbi, feed me.
I said to him: Wait
until I unload from the donkey.
I had not managed to unload the donkey
before his soul left him.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לָהֶם בָּנַיי אֲנִי גָּרַמְתִּי לְעַצְמִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the students' question.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: His suffering is self-imposed, as atonement for delaying help to a starving poor man who then died.

steps.title: נחום prays for his own suffering
steps.stepSummary: נחום falls on the dead man and asks that his own eyes, hands, and legs be damaged, and finally that his whole body be covered in boils.
steps.simpleTranslation: I fell on his face and said: My eyes, which had no pity on your eyes, should be blinded. My hands, which had no pity on your hands, should be cut off. My legs, which had no pity on your legs, should be cut off. I was not at peace until I said: My whole body should be full of boils.
steps.whatsHappening: נחום finishes his story. His afflictions came from his own request, as a punishment that matches his failure.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each part of the body is punished measure for measure. His eyes did not look at the man's need, his hands did not give quickly, and his legs did not move quickly. This explains exactly the condition described in Step 15.

keyTerms.meaning: My mind was calmed / I was at peace

phrases.english: I went and fell upon his face,
and I said: My eyes,
which had no pity on your eyes, let them be blinded;

phrases.aramaic: יָדַיי שֶׁלֹּא חָסוּ עַל יָדֶיךָ — יִתְגַּדְּמוּ,
phrases.english: my hands, which had no pity on your hands, let them be cut off;

phrases.aramaic: רַגְלַי שֶׁלֹּא חָסוּ עַל רַגְלֶיךָ — יִתְקַטְּעוּ.
phrases.english: my legs, which had no pity on your legs, let them be amputated.
And my mind was not at rest
until I said:
My whole body should be full of boils.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָלַכְתִּי וְנָפַלְתִּי עַל פָּנָיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues his answer and explains how each affliction began.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: His blindness, missing limbs, and boils were afflictions he requested, measure for measure, as atonement.

steps.title: Woe to us, woe to me
steps.stepSummary: The students mourn seeing him this way. נחום says it would be worse if they did not see him this way, because the suffering atones for him.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: Woe to us that we see you like this! He said to them: Woe to me if you did not see me like this.
steps.whatsHappening: The first story ends with a short exchange that sums up its message.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The students see only the pain. נחום sees the suffering as a gift, because it cleans away his sin. Without it he would carry that guilt into the next world.

keyTerms.meaning: You saw me in this state

steps.whatToRemember: נחום איש גם זו chose his suffering as atonement for a small delay in helping a poor man. He welcomed it instead of resenting it.

phrases.english: They said to him: Woe to us
that we have seen you like this!
He said to them: Woe to me
if you had not seen me like this.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרוּ לוֹ אוֹי לָנוּ שֶׁרְאִינוּךָ בְּכָךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the story of his suffering.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Suffering that atones is a blessing, not a curse.

steps.title: Why was he called נחום איש גם זו?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks where his name 'גם זו' comes from.
steps.simpleTranslation: And why did they call him נחום איש גם זו?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns to a new question about his name. This sets up the next story.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The name might sound like it refers to a place called גם זו. The גמרא is about to explain it by his attitude instead.

phrases.english: And why did they call him
Nachum Ish Gam Zu?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאַמַּאי קָרוּ לֵיהּ נַחוּם אִישׁ גַּם זוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from his suffering to the meaning of his name.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The origin of the name 'גם זו'.

steps.title: He always said 'this too is for the good'
steps.stepSummary: Whatever happened to him, he said 'גם זו לטובה'.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because about everything that happened to him, he would say: This too is for the good.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the name comes from his constant phrase.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His name describes his trust in ה׳. This matches the previous story, where he saw even terrible suffering as good.

keyTerms.meaning: This too is for the good

phrases.english: Because every matter
that happened to him,
he said: This too is for the good.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּכׇל מִילְּתָא דַּהֲוָה סָלְקָא לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about the name.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: He was named for his habit of saying 'גם זו לטובה' about everything.

steps.title: The gift to the emperor is stolen
steps.stepSummary: The Jews send נחום to the קיסר with a chest of jewels. At an inn, people steal the jewels and fill the chest with dirt.
steps.simpleTranslation: Once the Jews wanted to send a gift to the emperor. They said: Who should go? Let נחום איש גם זו go, because he is used to miracles. They sent with him a chest full of jewels and pearls. He went and slept at an inn. At night the residents took everything from his chest and filled it with dirt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a story that shows his 'גם זו לטובה' attitude in action. This step sets up the problem.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He was chosen because miracles happen to him. Now the gift is ruined. Bringing a box of dirt to the emperor looks like an insult, so the danger is real.

phrases.english: One time, they wanted,
the Jews, to send a gift to the emperor's house.
They said: Who should go?
Let Nachum Ish Gam Zu go,
for he is accustomed to miracles.
They sent with him
a chest full of precious stones and pearls.
He went and spent the night at a certain inn.
At night those residents got up
and took the contents of his chest
and filled it with dirt.

steps.triggerLanguage: זִימְנָא חֲדָא בְּעוֹ לְשַׁדּוֹרֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל דּוֹרוֹן לְבֵי קֵיסָר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a story that illustrates the name.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The precious gift was stolen and replaced with dirt.

steps.title: The king finds dirt and wants to kill them
steps.stepSummary: At the palace the chest is opened and found full of dirt. The king wants to kill all the Jews, and נחום still says 'גם זו לטובה'.
steps.simpleTranslation: When he got there, they opened the chest and saw it was full of dirt. The king wanted to kill all of them. He said: The Jews are mocking me. נחום said: This too is for the good.
steps.whatsHappening: The danger peaks. Even facing death, נחום says 'גם זו לטובה'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the real test of his motto. He says it when there seems to be no good outcome at all.
steps.confusionAlert: In phrase 5 the speaker is the king (he accuses the Jews of mocking him). In phrase 6 the speaker is נחום. Both lines begin with 'אֲמַר', so pay attention to who is talking.

phrases.english: When he arrived there,
they opened the chest,
and saw that it was full of dirt.
The king wanted to kill all of them.
He said: The Jews are mocking me.
He said: This too is for the good.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי מְטָא הָתָם שְׁרִינְהוּ לְסִיפְטֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows the result of the theft.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Facing a death sentence, נחום still declares 'גם זו לטובה'.

steps.title: אליהו suggests the dirt is אברהם's miraculous dirt
steps.stepSummary: אליהו appears as one of the king's ministers. He suggests the dirt may be the dirt of אברהם, which turned into swords and arrows when thrown, and quotes a פסוק.
steps.simpleTranslation: אליהו came, looking like one of the king's men, and said to him: Perhaps this dirt is from the dirt of their father אברהם. When he threw dirt, it became swords, and when he threw straw, it became arrows, as it says: 'His sword makes them like dust, his bow like blown straw.'
steps.whatsHappening: The turning point of the story. אליהו gives the king a reason to see the dirt as a valuable weapon instead of an insult.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק in ישעיה is read as describing אברהם in his war against the kings, where dust and straw became weapons. If this is that dirt, the 'insult' is really a priceless gift. The story continues next.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows how 'גם זו לטובה' plays out: what looked like a disaster becomes the key to success.

phrases.english: Eliyahu came
and appeared to him as one of them (the ministers),
and said to him: Perhaps

phrases.aramaic: הָא עַפְרָא מֵעַפְרָא דְּאַבְרָהָם אֲבוּהוֹן הוּא,
phrases.english: this dirt is from the dirt of Avraham their father,

phrases.aramaic: דְּכִי הֲוָה שָׁדֵי עַפְרָא — הָווּ סַיְיפֵי,
phrases.english: for when he threw dirt, it became swords,
and straw became arrows,
as it is written: 'His sword makes them like dust,
his bow like driven straw' (Isaiah 41:2).

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲתָא אֵלִיָּהוּ אִדְּמִי לֵיהּ כְּחַד מִינַּיְיהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins turning the danger into salvation.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: אליהו proposes that the dirt is the miraculous dirt of אברהם, supported by ישעיה 41:2.

steps.title: The dirt works and נחום is sent home with honor
steps.stepSummary: The Romans test the dirt on a province they could not conquer, and it works. The king fills נחום's chest with jewels and sends him off with great honor.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was one province that they could not conquer. They tested some of the dirt on it and conquered it. They went into the king's treasury, filled נחום's chest with precious stones and pearls, and sent him off with great honor.
steps.whatsHappening: The story continues from אליהו's suggestion. The Romans try the dirt in battle, it really turns into weapons, and נחום is rewarded.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the payoff of אליהו's suggestion in step 26. The thing that looked like a disaster (dirt instead of jewels) turns out to save the Jews and bring honor, so נחום's motto 'גם זו לטובה' proves true.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the payoff of the whole story. It shows the reason behind נחום's name: what seemed bad really was 'for the good.'

phrases.english: There was one province
that they were unable to conquer
they tested some of it (the dirt) and conquered it
phrases.notes: They threw the dirt at the enemy, and it became weapons.

phrases.english: They entered his treasury
and filled his (נחום's) chest
with precious stones and pearls
and sent him off with great honor

steps.triggerLanguage: הַוְיָא חֲדָא מְדִינְתָּא דְּלָא מָצוּ לְמִיכְבְּשַׁהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Carries out אליהו's suggestion from Step 26: the dirt is tested and proves miraculous.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The dirt turned into weapons, the province was conquered, and נחום was honored and rewarded.

steps.title: The innkeepers ask נחום what he brought
steps.stepSummary: On the way home נחום stays at the same inn. The innkeepers ask what earned him such honor, and he answers, 'What I took from here, I brought there.'
steps.simpleTranslation: When he came back, he stayed overnight at that same inn. They said to him: 'What did you bring with you that they gave you so much honor?' He said to them: 'What I took from here, I brought there.'
steps.whatsHappening: נחום returns to the inn where his jewels were stolen. The innkeepers are curious, and his short answer sets up their mistake in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: נחום's answer is true: the dirt came from the inn. But the innkeepers wrongly think the dirt itself had magic power. They do not realize the miracle happened only in נחום's merit.

phrases.english: When they came, they lodged at that inn
They (the innkeepers) said to him:
What did you bring with you
that they gave you all this honor?
He said to them:
What I took from here, I brought there.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי אֲתוֹ, בִּיתוּ בְּהָהוּא דִּיּוּרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story: נחום is honored, and now the thieves from Step 24 want to know why.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: נחום tells the innkeepers that he brought the emperor what he took from their inn.

steps.title: The innkeepers bring their dirt and are executed
steps.stepSummary: The innkeepers tear down their inn and bring its dirt to the king. They claim the miraculous dirt was theirs, but it fails when tested, and they are executed.
steps.simpleTranslation: They tore down their house and brought the dirt to the king's palace. They said to him: 'The dirt that was brought here came from our place.' They tested it and found nothing special, and the king killed those innkeepers.
steps.whatsHappening: The story ends. The greedy thieves try to cash in, but their dirt does not work and they are punished.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The failed test proves the miracle came from נחום's merit and not from the dirt. The people who stole from the righteous man are punished measure for measure.
steps.whatToRemember: The story of נחום איש גם זו shows that what looks like a disaster can really be for the good. Miracles come because of a person's merit, not because of the object involved.

phrases.english: They tore down their dwelling (inn)
and brought it (its dirt) to the king's palace
They said to him:
This dirt that was brought here
is from our (place).
They tested it, and it was not found (to work)
and they killed those residents.

steps.triggerLanguage: סְתַרוּ לְדִירַיְיהוּ וְאַמְטִינְהוּ לְבֵי מַלְכָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The innkeepers act on their misunderstanding of נחום's answer from Step 28.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The innkeepers' dirt had no power, showing the miracle came from נחום's merit, and they were put to death.

steps.title: Back to the משנה: what counts as a plague
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא returns to the משנה's question about what counts as a plague of דבר: a city that sends out 500 soldiers, and so on.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'What counts as דבר (a plague)? A city that sends out five hundred infantrymen, etc.'
steps.whatsHappening: The story is over, and the גמרא goes back to the next line of the משנה. This line only quotes the משנה to set up the ברייתא that explains it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה rules that the community sounds an alarm and fasts during a plague. It therefore has to define when a plague officially exists. In a city of 500 men, three deaths on three days in a row counts as a plague.

keyTerms.meaning: A city that sends out (soldiers), a way of measuring its population
Etc., the rest of the quote

steps.confusionAlert: 'Sends out 500 infantrymen' does not mean the city is at war. It is simply a way of saying the city has 500 adult men.

phrases.english: What is (considered) a plague?

phrases.aramaic: — עִיר הַמּוֹצִיאָה חֲמֵשׁ מֵאוֹת רַגְלִי כּוּ׳.
phrases.english: A city that sends out five hundred infantrymen, etc.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי זוֹ הִיא דֶּבֶר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the story and returns to the משנה's legal discussion.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The משנה defines a plague based on the size of the city and the pattern of deaths.

steps.title: A ברייתא: the rule for a city of 1,500 men
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא rules that a city of 1,500 men, like כפר עכו, is in a plague if nine people die over three days in a row.
steps.simpleTranslation: תנו רבנן: A city that sends out 1,500 infantrymen, such as כפר עכו, where nine dead were carried out over three days in a row, has a plague.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that expands the משנה's rule to a bigger city. It shows that the number of deaths grows with the size of the city.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The measure is proportional: one death per day for every 500 men. A city three times bigger needs three times the deaths, which means three per day over three days. The ברייתא adds the larger-city case and makes this ratio clear.
steps.confusionAlert: Nine deaths over three days means three deaths each day. It does not mean nine deaths in total spread out any way at all.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:

phrases.aramaic: עִיר הַמּוֹצִיאָה חֲמֵשׁ מֵאוֹת וְאֶלֶף רַגְלִי,
phrases.english: A city that sends out fifteen hundred infantrymen
such as the village of Akko
and nine dead were carried out of it
over three days, one after another
this is a plague.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: עִיר הַמּוֹצִיאָה חֲמֵשׁ מֵאוֹת וְאֶלֶף רַגְלִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains and expands the משנה quoted in Step 30.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In a city of 1,500 men, nine deaths over three consecutive days (three per day) counts as a plague.

steps.title: Deaths on one day or over four days do not count
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא adds that nine deaths all on one day, or spread over four days, are not a plague.
steps.simpleTranslation: If they died on one day, or over four days, this is not a plague.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא now sets the limits of its rule. The pattern of deaths matters, not only the total number.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A plague is defined by a steady daily pattern of deaths. One bad day could be a single disaster, and spreading the deaths over four days lowers the daily rate below the measure. So the same nine deaths do not count in either case.

phrases.english: (If they died) on one day, or over four days
this is not a plague.

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּיוֹם אֶחָד אוֹ בְּאַרְבָּעָה יָמִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Sets the boundaries of the rule given in Step 31.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Nine deaths all on one day, or spread over four days, do not count as a plague.

steps.title: The rule for a city of 500 men
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא repeats the משנה's case: in a city of 500 men, like כפר עמיקו, three deaths over three days in a row is a plague.
steps.simpleTranslation: And a city that sends out 500 infantrymen, such as כפר עמיקו, where three dead were carried out over three days in a row, has a plague.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא finishes by stating the smaller-city case, which matches the משנה. It gives a real example of such a city.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This confirms the ratio of one death per day for every 500 men. Placing the two cases side by side shows the measure is based on population and not on a fixed number of deaths.

keyTerms.meaning: And (the dead) were carried out of it

steps.whatToRemember: A plague (דבר) means one death per day, for three days in a row, for every 500 men in the city. Deaths all on one day, or spread over more days, do not count.

phrases.english: And a city that sends out five hundred infantrymen
such as the village of Amiko
and three dead were carried out of it
over three days, one after another
this is a plague.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְעִיר הַמּוֹצִיאָה חֲמֵשׁ מֵאוֹת רַגְלִי, כְּגוֹן כְּפַר עֲמִיקוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the ברייתא with the smaller-city case, matching the משנה from Step 30.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In a city of 500 men, three deaths over three consecutive days counts as a plague.
